cover.headline: India's third-largest hospital chain is born: the merger is accretive on paper, but at ₹697 the price already assumes the synergies arrive
cover.lead: On 1-Jul-2026 Quality Care India (Blackstone's CARE Hospitals, KIMSHEALTH and Evercare) merged into Aster DM Healthcare, which had sold its Gulf business in 2024. The new **Aster DM Quality Care** runs 39 hospitals with 10,898 beds, two-thirds of them outside metros, and is jointly controlled by the Moopen family (~24%) and Blackstone (~31%). We value the **merged company**, because that is what each of the 87.17 cr shares now owns; standalone Aster is a scenario. Pro-forma revenue rose 20% and operating EBITDA 30% in Q1FY27 before any synergies, and management targets a 24-25% margin by FY28-29. We forecast EBITDA of ₹2,402 / 2,883 / 3,394 cr and EPS of ₹12.0 / 14.5 / 17.0 for FY27-29E (pro-forma, full years), below most of the street on revenue. The street values the stock on **EV/EBITDA on FY28E**; applying **23x to Sep-28E EBITDA after minorities (20.5x consolidated EBITDA of ₹3,139 cr)**, net of debt and leases, gives **{{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): we initiate with HOLD.** Cross-checks: P/E ₹723, DCF ₹437. Bull {{scen.bull.tp|inr}}; bear {{scen.bear.tp|inr}}.

arguments.p: Aster brought Kerala and Bengaluru (Medcity, CMI, MIMS); QCIL brought Hyderabad, Trivandrum, central and eastern India and Bangladesh. Kerala is still 43% of beds, but no state is a majority. Q1FY27 pro-forma: occupancy 64% (+5.1pp), ARPP IP ₹1,36,802 (+10%), payor mix 87% cash and insurance.

arguments.h: Accretive at equal multiples, but QCIL's numbers are thin
arguments.p: QCIL contributed 53% of FY26 operating EBITDA for 42.7% of the shares, so pro-forma EPS rises from ₹7.49 (Aster) to ₹8.94. But QCIL's interest, depreciation and minorities are not published, its numbers are unaudited, and ~11% of combined EBITDA belongs to minority partners.

arguments.h: Growth is visible; synergies are a promise
arguments.p: Bed plan +4,179 to 15,077 by FY30 (53% brownfield) for ~₹4,700 cr of project capex; synergy target ₹150-200 cr. We model revenue +{{F.salesGrowth.0|pct}} / +{{F.salesGrowth.1|pct}} / +{{F.salesGrowth.2|pct}} and a post-Ind AS margin of {{F.ebitdaMargin.0|pct}} → {{F.ebitdaMargin.2|pct}}, the low end of guidance.

At ₹697 the stock trades at 24.7x our FY28E EBITDA after minorities, close to its 25.9x median since the deal; peers had de-rated 11% by 30-Sep-2026, giving 23x and {{dcf.tp|inr}}. The street (₹855-920, average ₹898) pays ~27-31x; our DCF (₹437) says even today's price needs the expansion to work.

catalysts: Q2FY27 results (due by mid-November 2026): the first accounts with QCIL consolidated, showing the real interest, depreciation, minorities and pooling adjustments behind our pro-forma estimates.
Synergy delivery: management targets ₹150-200 cr (10-15% of FY24 pro-forma EBITDA), starting in FY27 and meaningful from FY28.
Openings: Aster Capital, Trivandrum (454 beds, ~Jan-2027), Hyderabad women & children (300, ~Apr-2027), Sarjapur phase I (460, H2FY28), and QCIL brownfield blocks by 2028.
Regulation: follow-up to the Supreme Court's 30-Sep-2026 remarks on drug mark-ups by corporate hospitals (a uniform 16% trade margin was suggested).
Share supply: TPG (~3% left after its August sale) and, over time, Blackstone (~31%) are financial owners that will sell.

sections.title: Multi-specialty hospitals in South, Central and East India, plus labs and a brand-licensed pharmacy chain

blocks.p: Aster DM Quality Care runs **39 hospitals** (10,898 capacity and 10,559 operational beds at June 2026), 321 labs and patient-experience centres and the Aster brand on 205 pharmacies run by an associate company. Almost all revenue (~97%) comes from hospitals and clinics: in-patient treatment (cardiac, oncology, neurosciences, gastroenterology, orthopaedics, transplants) and out-patient care. It has **four brands**: **Aster** (Medcity Kochi, MIMS in north Kerala, CMI/RV/Whitefield in Bengaluru, Ramesh in Andhra), **CARE Hospitals** (Hyderabad, Vizag, Nagpur, Raipur, Bhubaneswar, Indore and others), **KIMSHEALTH** (Trivandrum and south Kerala) and **Evercare** (Dhaka and Chattogram, Bangladesh). Kerala is the core: 4,642 beds and ~53% of Aster's hospital revenue, with a ~25% margin.

The two halves were similar in size in FY26: Aster ₹4,643 cr revenue and ₹947 cr operating EBITDA (20.4%), QCIL ₹4,630 cr and ₹1,066 cr (23.0%). Patients pay mostly in cash (53%) or through corporate and insurance cover (34%); government schemes are 9% and international patients (medical value travel) 4%. About 65% of beds are in tier-2 and tier-3 cities, where competition is thinner and land cheaper, but prices are lower than in metros.

blocks.callout: **What this does to the history:** Screener's data before FY23 includes the Gulf business (FY22 revenue ₹10,253 cr vs ₹2,994 cr for India alone in FY23), FY25 profit includes a ₹4,981 cr post-tax gain on the sale (EPS ₹107.66), and FY26 is Aster alone (₹388 cr profit, EPS ₹7.49 on 51.81 cr shares). Screener also books the ₹374 cr equity component of convertible preference shares as debt and its FY26 "net profit" (₹427 cr) is before minorities. We put profit on the after-minorities basis, neutralise the ₹374 cr in our net-debt figure and, because the merger took effect on 1-Jul-2026, put FY26 on a **pro-forma combined basis** (₹9,273 cr revenue, EPS ₹8.94 on 87.17 cr shares) as the model's base year. Per-share and multiple history before the deal describes a different company, so our valuation history starts at the merger announcement (29-Nov-2024).

sections.title: The merger is done: we value the merged company; standalone Aster is a scenario

exhibit.title: Terms and timeline
head: Item
Detail
rows: Step 1 (share swap): Aster bought 5.0% of QCIL (1,90,46,028 shares at ₹445.83) from BCP (Blackstone) and TPG, paying with 1,86,07,969 new Aster shares at ₹456.33 (46,51,992 to TPG, 1,39,55,977 to BCP); completed in FY26 (share capital 49.95 -> 51.81 cr shares). Step 2: QCIL amalgamated into Aster by a scheme at 977 Aster shares for every 1,000 QCIL shares.

Issue price ₹456.33 = SEBI ICDR pricing (higher of 90- and 10-day VWAP to 28-Nov-2024); QCIL value ₹445.83 a share. Equity values used: Aster ₹22,794 cr, QCIL ₹16,983 cr; inter-se split 57.3% Aster holders / 42.7% QCIL holders. The deal valued Aster at 36.6x FY24 adjusted post-Ind AS EV/EBITDA and QCIL at 25.2x. No cash consideration ('cash neutral'). Expected post-merger holding: Aster promoters 24.0%, Blackstone (BCP Asia II Topco IV) 30.7%, Aster public 33.3%, other QCIL holders 12.0%. Aster promoters and Blackstone are joint promoters with 3 board nominees each; independent directors at least half the board; BCP's rights fall away below 10%, the Moopen family's below 5%.

CCI approval 15-Apr-2025; NSE/BSE no-objection 6-Oct-2025; NCLT application 11-Dec-2025; NCLT order convening meetings 21-Jan-2026; shareholders approved 10-Mar-2026 with 96.68% of votes in favour; NCLT Hyderabad sanctioned the scheme 19-Jun-2026; record date 9-Jul-2026.

Pooling of interests under Ind AS 103 (scheme clause 17.1): QCIL's assets and liabilities are combined at book value, so no large new goodwill and book equity rises only by QCIL's book equity.

10-15% of FY24 pro-forma EBITDA, i.e. ₹150-200 cr, from procurement, clinical talent and programmes, IT, indirect costs, capex efficiency and medical value travel; management says none were in the Q1FY27 numbers and they start in FY27, more meaningfully from FY28.
19-Aug-2026: TPG's Centella Mauritius sold ~6.66% at an average ₹766.17 (₹4,451 cr block); 2-Sep-2026: promoter entity Union (Mauritius) Holdings bought 46,09,800 shares (0.52%) at ₹760 (₹350 cr).

blocks.p: **Which entity do we value?** The merged one. On 30-Sep-2026 the merger had been effective for three months, the 35.36 cr new shares were listed, QCIL had ceased to exist and the company was reporting the two businesses as one. A share bought at ₹697 is 1/87.17 crore of the combined company, so valuing Aster alone on 51.81 cr shares would answer a question nobody can trade. We show standalone Aster below as a scenario, because it tells us whether the merger added value for Aster's old shareholders.

blocks.callout: **So what:** at the same multiple, the merged company is worth ~27% more per share than Aster alone would be, because QCIL brought 53% of combined operating EBITDA for 42.7% of the shares. That is the accretion management promised. The flip side: in November 2024 the deal valued Aster at 36.6x FY24 EBITDA and QCIL at 25.2x; today the market pays ~25x forward for the combination, so Aster's old shareholders swapped a richly valued stock for a larger, cheaper one with more debt, more minorities and a private-equity co-owner.

sections.title: Private hospitals: consolidation, pricier care and expansion into smaller cities, with regulation as the cloud

blocks.p: Indian private hospitals are in a growth-and-consolidation phase: listed chains are adding beds at record pace, private equity has built platforms (Blackstone's Quality Care: CARE Hospitals + KIMSHEALTH + Evercare) and is now merging them into listed companies, insurance is a rising share of payment, and tier-2/3 cities are the new battleground. Prices rise with case mix (robotics, transplants, oncology). The counterweights are regulation (price caps, drug mark-ups, government-scheme rates), doctor costs and competition in Bengaluru and Hyderabad.

sections.title: Revenue = beds × occupancy × price: occupancy +5pp and price/mix +7% drove Q1FY27

blocks.p: Hospital revenue is the product of **operational beds**, **occupancy** (share of beds filled) and **revenue per occupied bed-day** (ARPOB). The company now reports occupancy on census beds and ARPP IP (revenue per in-patient) rather than a combined ARPOB, so we compute an **implied ARPOB on operational beds**: hospital and clinic revenue ÷ (operational beds × days × occupancy). In Q1FY27 that was ₹41,222 (₹2,535 cr over 10,559 beds at 64%), against ~₹38,600 for FY26. The year-on-year jump in Q1FY27 came from both levers: operational beds +3.6% (Kasargod, Whitefield Block D, Ongole), occupancy +5.1pp and ARPP IP +10% (more robotics, transplants and joint replacements; ALOS down 2% to 3.4 days).

blocks.callout: **What would move the numbers:** each 1pp of occupancy on 10,559 beds is ~38,500 bed-days a year, or ~₹160 cr of revenue at FY27E prices (~₹60-70 cr of EBITDA at incremental margins). Our forecasts take the existing network from 64% to 68.5% by FY29E; Kerala already runs at 64% and QCIL at 65%, so the room is real but not unlimited.

sections.title: Mature hospitals earn ~30% margins; a quarter of the beds earn under 15%

blocks.p: From Q1FY27 the company sorts its hospitals into four buckets. **Mature** (3+ years old, margin 25%+): 65% of beds, 73% of hospital revenue, 86% of hospital EBITDA, at a 29.7% margin. **Focus** (3+ years, 15-25% margin): 14% of beds at 16.8%. **Emerging** (under 3 years): 10% of beds, revenue +63%, margin 12.4% (Kasargod broke even in nine months). **Under-performing** (3+ years, below 15%): 11% of beds at 3.6%. Hospital-level EBITDA was ₹639 cr (25.2%) before ~₹60 cr of corporate costs and other businesses.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** this is the most useful disclosure the merger has produced. If the focus and under-performing hospitals (25% of beds) reached the mature margin, hospital EBITDA would rise by ~₹340 cr a year (Q1FY27 run-rate): that, more than procurement, is the real synergy. But these are often hospitals in hard local markets; we assume only part of the gap closes by FY29E.

sections.title: The next 4,179 beds: half brownfield, mostly in existing markets

blocks.p: Management plans to add ~4,179 beds to reach ~15,077 (FY27 634, FY28 1,190, FY29 1,555, FY30+ 800); 53% are additions to existing hospitals, which ramp faster and cost less (₹0.8-1.0 cr a bed vs ~₹1.5 cr greenfield). The big new hospitals are Aster's: Trivandrum (454 beds, owned, ~Jan-2027), a 300-bed women & children hospital in Hyderabad (~Apr-2027) and Sarjapur, Bengaluru (450+ beds; phase I H2FY28). QCIL's ~1,700 beds are mostly brownfield blocks (Bhubaneswar, Raipur, Kottayam, Nagercoil, Banjara Hills) plus a greenfield in Indore. Planned spending: ~₹2,700 cr (Aster) + ~₹2,000 cr (QCIL) over 3-4 years.

sections.title: Competitive advantage: strong in Kerala and in complex care; scale benefits still to be proven

verdicts: 4,642 beds in Kerala after adding KIMSHEALTH (Trivandrum) to Aster Medcity, MIMS Kozhikode/Kannur/Kottakkal; Kerala cluster margin ~25% and occupancy 64% (Q1FY27).
Pricing power and doctor pull in the home market.
Transplants, robotics (1,300+ robotic cases at Aster in FY26), DBS and liver programmes that can now be shared across 39 hospitals; Aster CMI and Medcity ranked #12 and #28 in India (Newsweek 2026).
Supports case mix and ARPP growth of 7-10% a year.
Third-largest listed chain by beds; QCIL saved ~₹85 cr through central procurement in FY26; merger synergies targeted at ₹150-200 cr.
Real but not yet proven for the merged group (none in Q1FY27).
87% cash and corporate/insurance, 9% government schemes, 4% international (Q1FY27).
Less exposed to scheme tariffs than many peers.
Four brands (Aster, CARE, KIMSHEALTH, Evercare) with local strength; the Aster name is shared with a Gulf company the group no longer owns (35% Moopen-owned).
No single national brand; rebranding decisions pending.
Competitive metros: Aster lost doctors in Karnataka in FY26; CARE's Hyderabad assets needed turnarounds; Hyderabad and Sarjapur are new greenfields.
Growth here has to be bought with doctors and capex.
₹1-1.5 cr a bed; ~₹4,700 cr of announced expansion over 3-4 years; company ROCE (excl. CWIP, intangibles) 22.9% but return on total capital far lower because of goodwill from acquisitions.
Returns depend on filling new beds.

blocks.title: Moat scorecard
blocks.source: GAM research compilation (company filings and calls to Sep-2026)

blocks.callout: **Honest verdict:** there is a real moat in Kerala, where Aster and KIMSHEALTH together run ~4,600 beds with doctor franchises and international referral networks that new entrants cannot copy quickly, and in quaternary programmes that need scale to staff. Elsewhere the group is one of several strong local players (CARE in Hyderabad competes with Apollo, KIMS, Yashoda; Aster in Bengaluru with Manipal, Narayana, Fortis). Merging two regional chains does not by itself create pricing power: the benefits are cost and talent sharing, and those still have to be shown.

sections.title: Two businesses of equal size: combined revenue up 13% a year and margins up 2.6pp since FY24

blocks.p: The company that trades today did not exist as one set of accounts until July 2026, so we show two histories. **Aster alone** (reported): revenue grew from ₹2,994 cr in FY23 (India only, after the Gulf business was carved out) to ₹4,643 cr in FY26, 16% a year, and its operating EBITDA margin rose from 15.0% to 20.4% as Kerala recovered and Bengaluru matured. **Quality Care (QCIL)**, Blackstone's CARE + KIMSHEALTH + Evercare platform, grew from ₹3,615 cr to ₹4,630 cr over FY24-26 with a higher margin (21.5% → 23.0%). **Combined**, revenue grew 13% a year (₹7,314 cr → ₹9,273 cr) and operating EBITDA 20% a year (₹1,396 cr → ₹2,013 cr). These are the company's pro-forma figures, unaudited, and QCIL's include KIMSHEALTH for the full year although it was bought in Q4FY24.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** on paper the merger is accretive: QCIL brought 53% of combined FY26 operating EBITDA for 42.7% of the shares, and EPS on the pro-forma basis rises from ₹7.49 to ₹8.94. The catch is quality: QCIL's below-EBITDA lines (interest, depreciation, minorities) are not published, so the pro-forma profit relies on our estimates, and the first combined quarterly accounts (Q2FY27, due by mid-November 2026) will test them.

sections.title: Pro-forma quarters: revenue +20% and margin +1.7pp in Q1FY27, before any synergies

blocks.p: On a combined basis the business has accelerated through FY26: revenue growth reached 20% in Q1FY27 (₹2,597 cr) and operating EBITDA 30% (₹576 cr), with occupancy up 5.1pp to 64%. Both halves contributed: Aster revenue +22% (Kerala +25% after a weak FY25, Karnataka back to +16% after re-hiring doctors) and QCIL +19% (occupancy 65.4%, +6.6pp). Management stresses that none of this is merger synergy; the two companies ran separately until 1-Jul-2026.

sections.title: A ₹4,700 cr expansion over 3-4 years, funded from operating cash; returns on tangible capital are good

blocks.p: Aster generated ₹656 cr of operating cash in FY26 and spent ₹549 cr on capex (45% on expansion). The merged plan is far bigger: Aster ~₹2,700 cr for ~2,500 beds over four years (₹350 cr already spent), QCIL ~₹2,000 cr for ~1,700 beds over 3-4 years (₹1-1.1 cr a bed; brownfield ₹0.8-1.0 cr, greenfield ₹1.5 cr), plus maintenance capex of ~5% of revenue. We model ₹1,550 / 1,900 / 2,000 cr in FY27-29E including ~₹100 cr a year of new leases. Operating cash (~₹1,500-2,200 cr a year) roughly covers it, so net debt stays near ₹3,000 cr including leases (~1x EBITDA).

blocks.callout: **The capital question:** company ROCE (21-23%) excludes goodwill and work in progress. On all the capital investors have put in, including the goodwill from QCIL's own acquisitions (KIMSHEALTH, Evercare) carried at book under pooling, our ROE is only ~12-14% in FY27-29E. The new beds have to earn well above the ~11.6% cost of capital for the expansion to create value; Kasargod (breakeven in nine months) and Nagercoil (~30% margin in ~18 months) are encouraging examples.

sections.title: Earnings quality: clean at Aster, untested at the merged level

bullets: **Pro-forma, not audited.** QCIL's numbers are "indicative and subject to statutory audit adjustments"; the merged accounts start in Q2FY27 and pooling of interests may restate comparatives. Our FY26 base uses estimates for QCIL's depreciation, interest, tax and minorities (see gaps).

**Three EBITDA definitions.** Company "operating EBITDA" (₹2,013 cr pro-forma FY26) excludes ESOP cost and variable O&M fees on asset-light hospitals (₹45 cr at Aster in FY26); reported post-Ind AS EBITDA is lower (Aster ₹901 cr vs ₹947 cr operating); pre-Ind AS (after rent) lower still (₹788 cr). Rent sits in depreciation and interest under Ind AS 116.

**Minorities matter.** KIMSHEALTH's founder keeps 15-20%, several Aster and CARE hospitals have partners; brokers put minorities at 10-13% of EBITDA. We value EBITDA after minorities and model minorities inside the tax line.
**Associates lose money.** The Aster pharmacies are run by Alfaone (~49% owned), which cost ₹37 cr in FY26 and needs Aster's support letter.

**Exceptionals every year.** FY25: ₹4,981 cr GCC gain; FY26: ₹38 cr income (minimum-wage reversal) and ₹71 cr expenses (merger costs, CSR on the GCC gain); Q1FY27: ₹114 cr merger costs. We exclude them.
**Cash conversion.** Aster's operating cash flow was 73% of post-Ind AS EBITDA in FY26 (₹656 cr); receivables are short (~24 days) because cash and insurance dominate.

**Screener quirks.** Its FY26 net profit (₹427 cr) is before minorities and it books ₹374 cr of preference-share equity reserve as debt; we use profit after minorities and neutralise the ₹374 cr in our net-debt figure (ASTERDM.patch.js).

blocks.callout: **Accounting flag: AMBER.** Aster itself reports cleanly (detailed KPIs, both EBITDA bases, Deloitte audit). The amber is for the transition: unaudited QCIL figures, a pooling accounting choice for a merger of two unrelated groups, large minorities and recurring "exceptional" items. The Q2FY27 and FY27 accounts will tell whether pro-forma margins survive audit.

sections.title: Aster brought net cash, QCIL brought debt: combined net debt ₹1,162 cr before leases

blocks.p: At March 2026 Aster had ₹1,327 cr of cash against ₹701 cr of bank debt (net cash ₹626 cr), the remains of the Gulf sale proceeds, and ₹1,518 cr of lease liabilities, mostly on asset-light operate-and-manage hospitals. QCIL had net debt of ₹1,388 cr after paying ~₹672 cr of deferred consideration for its Bangladesh hospitals, plus ~₹270 cr of leases. Combined net debt was ₹763 cr at March 2026 and ₹1,162 cr at June 2026 (₹1,673 cr at QCIL less Aster's ₹511 cr net cash), or ~₹2,950 cr including leases: about 1.2x pro-forma EBITDA. Minorities (₹258 cr at Aster, ₹1,518 cr at QCIL at book) are a further claim on the group.

The bigger balance-sheet issue is minorities: about 11% of EBITDA belongs to partners in subsidiaries (KIMSHEALTH's founder keeps 15-20%), which we deduct in the valuation.

sections.title: Ownership: the Moopen family and Blackstone control ~54% jointly; funds were diluted by the merger

blocks.p: Before the merger the Moopen family owned 40.39% of Aster (Jun-2026), Indian institutions 27.65%, foreign investors 10.53% and the public 21.41%. The 35.36 cr shares issued to QCIL holders on 13-Jul-2026 changed the register: the family's stake fell to ~24% and Blackstone, which owned ~68% of QCIL, became a co-promoter with ~30-31%. The first pattern after the allotment (July 2026) shows promoters at 53.7%, foreign investors 10.3% and Indian institutions 16.5%. TPG received 9.90% and sold ~6.66% within weeks; the Moopen family bought 0.52% at ₹760 on 2-Sep-2026.

sections.title: Our forecasts: revenue ~16% a year, EBITDA ~20%, EPS ~24% as margins improve

blocks.p: We model the merged company on a pro-forma basis (twelve months of QCIL in every year), from a bed build: existing beds × occupancy × implied ARPOB, plus new beds and other income streams; the authoring script checks the build equals model revenue. EBITDA is post-Ind AS (rent excluded), so leases count as debt and new leases are added to capex. Depreciation is 9.0% of the Aster gross block plus new capex (QCIL assets sit outside the gross block in the pro-forma base because the Excel model reads the Aster block from Screener, so the rate is high and D&A conservative), finance cost ₹330-350 cr, tax plus minorities plus associates ~34-35% of PBT, payout 25%. blocks.p: Every note with a disclosed method values the merged company on **EV/EBITDA on FY28E or 12-month-forward EBITDA** (27-32x). sections.title: Our honest summary: a good merger at a full price; buy on delivery or on weakness

blocks.callout: **What you are buying:** India's third-largest listed hospital chain, with a dominant Kerala franchise, strong complex-care programmes, 87% cash-and-insurance payors, a 15,000-bed plan that is half brownfield, and a margin path to ~24% that needs no heroics, run by a professional CEO under joint founder and Blackstone control.

**What you are paying:** 24.7x our FY28E EBITDA after minorities and 48.2x FY28E EPS, about the 25.9x and 52.1x it has averaged since the deal, at a time when listed peers trade ~11% below their own five-year medians. On the street's method and our inputs the target is {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): a HOLD. The DCF (₹437) is the warning: the price already assumes the expansion and synergies work for a long time.

sections.title: Glossary

exhibit.title: Terms used in this report
head: Term
What it means
rows: Quality Care India Ltd: Blackstone- and TPG-owned hospital group (CARE Hospitals, KIMSHEALTH, Evercare Bangladesh) that merged into Aster on 1-Jul-2026.
Aster's former Gulf hospitals, clinics and pharmacies, sold in April 2024 to a Fajr Capital-led consortium in which the Moopen family holds 35%.
Court (NCLT)-approved merger; QCIL holders received 977 Aster shares for every 1,000 QCIL shares.
Merger accounting that adds the two companies' assets and liabilities at book value, without revaluing them or creating new goodwill.
Figures shown as if the two companies had always been combined; unaudited.
Beds built vs beds open and staffed vs in-patient beds used to measure occupancy (excluding ICU, day-care and similar beds).
Average revenue per occupied bed-day. Implied ARPOB (ours) = hospital revenue ÷ (operational beds × days × occupancy).
Average revenue per in-patient: the company's preferred price measure.
Average length of stay (days) per in-patient.
Cardiac, oncology, neurosciences, gastroenterology, orthopaedics and transplants: the high-value specialties.
Company buckets: 3+ years old with 25%+ margin / 15-25% / under 3 years old / 3+ years with under 15%.
New beds added to an existing hospital / a new hospital on a new site.
Hospitals Aster operates and manages for owners for a fee, without owning the building.
Company measure: post-Ind AS EBITDA before ESOP cost, variable O&M fees and one-offs.
EBITDA after deducting rent (pre-Ind AS) vs before rent (post-Ind AS, as reported; rent then appears as depreciation and interest).
Shares of subsidiaries owned by others (e.g., KIMSHEALTH's founder); their share of profit and EBITDA is not shareholders'.
Enterprise value (market value plus net debt, here including leases) ÷ EBITDA; share price ÷ earnings per share.
A multiple computed on the merged company (all 87.17 cr shares, combined net debt and EBITDA) for dates before the merger took effect.
Half of FY28E plus half of FY29E: the 12-month-forward earnings the market will look at in September 2027.
Discounted cash flow; WACC is the required annual return used to discount future cash (here the cost of equity, 11.6%; net debt is small).
exhibit.source: GAM Research
